passage:
Dear Abhinav,
I'm writing because I can't say this out loud. Last week at the youth circle I asked why one rule is followed the way it is. I wasn't mocking anything; I really wanted to know. Two elders said I was disrespectful, and since then people look away when I walk in. Nobody sits with me. It hurts far more than I expected, and I keep thinking of quitting altogether. But yesterday my Nana's old friend, Mr Fazal, said, "A question is not an insult." I nearly cried with relief. Maybe those two elders are not the whole community. Thank you for not laughing when I told you.
Yusuf

qa.q: What happened after Yusuf asked the question at the youth circle?
qa.a: Two elders called Yusuf disrespectful, and people started looking away when Yusuf walked in.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling after being shunned, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Yusuf was deeply hurt and isolated; "It hurts far more than I expected" and "Nobody sits with me" show it. 🤍
Keep talking with open-minded people such as Mr Fazal and Abhinav, and remember that two elders are not the whole community.

qa.q: How might the two elders have seen Yusuf's question?
qa.a: As disrespect toward what they hold dear; they called it disrespectful, though Yusuf says it was honest curiosity.

grounding: Yusuf asks a doubtful question, is shunned and hurt by elders, and finds an open-minded elder without treating the group as the whole faith.

passage:
Saturday night

I asked one question at the satsang today, and now half the aunties won't look at me.

We were reading the story of the goddess, and I asked, "Do we believe this happened, or is it a way of teaching?" I really wanted to know. Mala aunty said, loudly, "Such disrespect. This is what English schools do." After that nobody passed me the prasad plate. I sat there with my face burning. On the way out, two of them turned away.

I cried in the auto. I felt like they'd thrown me out of something I've belonged to since I was small.

I called Elizabeth. She listened for a long time. Then she said, "At my church there are people like that, and people who love questions. Don't let the loudest ones be the whole thing."

That made me think of Padma paati, who runs the Tuesday study group and always says, "Ask, ask." I'm going to ask her tomorrow.

Sangeeta

qa.q: What question did Sangeeta ask at the satsang?
qa.a: Sangeeta asked, "Do we believe this happened, or is it a way of teaching?"

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling in the auto on the way home?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt deeply hurt and rejected, as if thrown out of something Sangeeta had belonged to since childhood.

qa.q: What is a wise next step for Sangeeta?
qa.a: Talking to Padma paati, an open-minded elder who welcomes questions, is wise because it keeps one group of aunties from standing for the whole faith.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth see what happened?
qa.a: Elizabeth understands it from her own church, and sees that a few loud people do not speak for everyone in a faith.

grounding: It shows a teen called disrespectful and shunned by elders for a doubtful question, who is hurt and then seeks an open-minded elder and a friend rather than treating one group as the whole faith.

passage:
Divyansh: they literally stopped talking to me
Sonali: who?
Divyansh: the uncles at the family path. i asked why we can't question some teachings
Divyansh: tauji said i'm "insulting the family." everyone went silent. nobody said bye when i left
Sonali: ugh. i'm sorry
Divyansh: i feel like i'm not allowed in anymore. it really hurt
Sonali: that's awful. but remember Bua?
Divyansh: which bua
Sonali: Nirmala bua. she's more religious than all of them and she loves arguing about meanings
Divyansh: oh ya. she once said doubt is part of faith
Sonali: exactly. call her. and there's that youth discussion circle at the temple near my college. they actually want questions
Divyansh: really?
Sonali: ya. tauji is not the whole religion 🙂
Divyansh: ok. i'll call bua tomorrow

qa.q: What did Tauji say Divyansh was doing?
qa.a: Tauji said Divyansh was "insulting the family."

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling after nobody said bye?
qa.a: Divyansh felt deeply hurt and shut out, as if no longer allowed to belong.

qa.q: Which suggestion from Sonali is wise, and why?
qa.a: Calling Nirmala Bua and trying the youth discussion circle is wise, because they welcome questions and show that one group of uncles is not the whole faith.

qa.q: How might Nirmala Bua feel if Divyansh calls her?
qa.a: Nirmala Bua would likely feel glad and welcoming, since she loves arguing about meanings and sees doubt as part of faith.

grounding: It shows a teen shunned by elders for a doubtful question, deeply hurt, who is guided towards an open-minded elder and group rather than treating one group as the whole faith.
